title: SWCraft editing-protocol test vector
description: The envelope every file under packages/tools/tests/fixtures/contracts/editing-protocol/examples/ and .../negative/ follows. A vector is a self-describing exchange — baseline assumptions, the request, and what must come back — not an annotated snippet, so Phases 19.2 and 19.3 receive executable acceptance inputs instead of prose with labels.
$comment: The relative reference `protocol.schema.json#/...` resolves against this document's $id, whose last path segment equals this file's name on disk; the consistency test builds a `referencing` registry over the two local files under exactly those identifiers.

name.description: A stable identifier for the vector, unique across both directories. Not the file name — the file may be renamed, the vector name may not.

description.description: What the vector proves, in one or two sentences.

kind.description: `example` files live under examples/ and state an accepted exchange; `negative` files live under negative/ and state a rejection.

input.description: The protocol request. Constrained by the conditional branches below: for an example and for a `semantic` negative it must conform to protocol.schema.json's request shapes; for a `protocol-schema` negative it is arbitrary JSON, because violating that schema is the whole point of the vector.
input.$comment: Any JSON here; the allOf branches narrow it.

allOf.$comment: An example is an accepted exchange: its input is a well-formed request and its expectation is a response shape.
Every negative expects an error, whichever layer detects it.

A `semantic` negative is a well-formed request whose violation only the 19.2 engine can find — an undeclared field, an illegal emitted identifier, a dangling reference, a stale baseline, an unapproved delta. The envelope therefore holds it to the protocol request shapes.

A `protocol-schema` negative is rejected by protocol.schema.json itself, so its input is admitted as arbitrary JSON here and its expectation is pinned to `schema-violation`. The test asserts the FACT of rejection only: a jsonschema ValidationError has no stable mapping to an error code, so no message text is matched.

context.description: The baseline assumptions the vector is stated against: what the model already holds, which baseline token the request carries, and what the approved scope covers. A negative's violation lives in this context or in the request, machine-checkably — never in a free-text label. `layers_present` and `existing_elements` together are the FIXTURE SPEC: a 19.2/19.3 harness builds the baseline model from them, and packages/tools/tests/test_editing_protocol_contracts.py (class `TestContextIsAFixtureSpec`) holds them to that reading rather than treating them as decoration.

summary.description: The starting state in prose, for a reader.

layers_present.description: The layers that exist in the baseline model. Its absence means no particular layer set is assumed either way; state it when the vector depends on it. When present it must cover every layer `existing_elements` names — a fixture cannot hold an element of a layer it does not have.

existing_elements.description: Elements the baseline model already holds, as addresses — the referenced targets, the identity a `create` collides with, the element an `update` addresses. Load-bearing rather than illustrative: a `create` in `input` whose address is listed here is an `identity-conflict` by construction, and one whose address is NOT listed is the accepted case, so the two may not disagree. One exception: a member of a `whole_value` LIST, because such a collection is a multiset and an address listed here may legally be created again — that adds a second occurrence rather than colliding. An address in `occupied_targets` is not an exception to this rule but an instance of its accepted case: its identity is free, so it is not listed here.

occupied_targets.description: Element addresses whose PLAIN storage file name — the one the registry composes from the identity — is already held by a file although NO element of that layer declares that identity. The second, narrower half of the fixture spec, reachable whenever a file is not named after the element it holds: a hand-authored file whose basename is not the name it declares, or, on a case-insensitive filesystem, a file whose name differs from the identity only in case. A `create` at an address listed here is the ACCEPTED case: the store never lets a file-name collision touch an element, so the new element's file takes the nearest free collision suffix (`~1`, `~2`, …) — which is storage and appears in no response — and only an identity `existing_elements` lists is an `identity-conflict`. It is stated separately because the fixture that produces it is different (a file, not an element) and because a harness must be able to tell the two preconditions apart.

baseline_state.description: Whether the token the request carries still describes the real model. `stale` is what a stale-baseline vector states: the model moved after the token was read.

authorizationContext.description: The approved scope this exchange is judged against. An empty `approved_scope` is an explicit statement that nothing is approved — the unauthorized-delta case — and is not the same as omitting the field.

scopeEntry.description: One approved operation at one address. Scope is keyed by operation and address, never by MCP tool name.

expectedResponse.description: An example's expectation: the response shape the accepted exchange must produce. Narrowed to the nine SUCCESS shapes on purpose (a `read` is answered in one of four: one address, several — `readManyResponse` —, none, the model map, or a count — `countResponse`; a `find` in `findResponse` or, in its `text` form, `findTextResponse`, or, in its `for_requirement` form, `findCandidatesResponse`) — protocol.schema.json's `$defs/response` union also admits `errorResult`, so referencing it here would let a file under examples/ state a rejection while `kind: "example"` says the exchange is accepted. A rejection is a negative, and its expectation is `expectedError`.

expectedError.description: A negative's expectation: the stable code, its failure class, and the layer that detects the violation. `violation_layer` is the discriminator the envelope's conditional branches key on.

violation_layer.description: `protocol-schema`: protocol.schema.json rejects the input on its own. `semantic`: the input is a well-formed request and only the 19.2 engine, over the staged result, can detect the violation.

addresses.description: The address(es) the rejection names, where it has any.

additional.description: The SECONDARY violations the same rejection must report alongside the primary one, in the order `errorResult.additional` carries them. Present only on a vector whose point is that one round trip reports everything a `check-model` run would; absent means the primary is the only violation and `errorResult.additional` is omitted.

expectedAdditionalError.description: One secondary violation of `expectedError.additional` — the vector-side mirror of protocol.schema.json's `$defs/errorDetail`, minus the message, which is not contract.
